title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — September 14, 2026 (A Twelve-Day Gap Closes, and a Third Escalation in Hong Kong)
headline: Hong Kong falls 5.9 points after a court jailed three Tiananmen vigil leaders for up to seven years.
summary:
Research could not be completed for twelve days, from September 2 through September 13. Tonight's cycle closes that gap in one pass across 1,331 entities.

Hong Kong's score falls 5.9 points, from 32.8 to 26.9 of 100. A High Court sentenced three Tiananmen vigil organizers to five to seven years in prison. The judges said the case involved no violence. The United Nations Human Rights Office called the sentences regrettable. Hong Kong's government dismissed the criticism as smears. It is the third escalation in a pattern the benchmark has tracked since July.

Two more countries would cross a band boundary on tonight's evidence, but neither finding was confirmed. France measured ten points below its published score, mostly on evidence that predates this review window. The most widely reported protest turned out to have happened in September 2025, not this year, and was excluded before scoring. The one real in-window finding, a diplomatic retraction made under U.S. pressure, is not strong enough on its own to confirm a boundary crossing. Slovenia's new government scrapped its predecessor's arms embargo on Israel and welcomed the opening of Israel's first embassy in Slovenia. That finding is real, but no court, UN body, or international organization has yet confirmed it at the strength the benchmark requires before a crossing is filed.

Nepal's flood death toll climbed to 1,386 people, and the country's score has now measured below its published level for a second cycle running. Jamaica's housing-relief program is confirmed at 1.05 billion Jamaican dollars, about $6.6 million, for 268 homes. Syria's score holds at zero, the lowest score on the benchmark, as fuel prices rose sharply and protests spread with no relief announced for the poorest households.

Spain's score, measured independently tonight, lines up within six tenths of a point of a downgrade already filed on August 26 that is still awaiting a decision. Boeing's score is confirmed at 14.1 after a $3.1 million federal fine, paid back in January, became public only in September. The delay in disclosure, not new misconduct, is what this cycle records. None of tonight's findings changed a published ranking.

pipeline.queueHandling: Nineteen organizations were checked across the twelve-day catch-up window. One finding was filed and fifteen scores were confirmed unchanged. Two more findings would cross a published band on tonight's evidence but were not confirmed, because neither met the sourcing strength the benchmark requires before a boundary crossing is filed. One further finding corroborates a downgrade already filed on 26 August and was not filed a second time. None of tonight's findings changed a published ranking.

topSignals.title: Hong Kong Falls 5.9 Points as a Third Escalation Lands on a Pattern Tracked Since July
topSignals.whyItMatters: A court jailed three Tiananmen vigil leaders for years in a case it called non-violent. The United Nations called the sentences regrettable; Hong Kong's government called the criticism smears.
topSignals.description: On 11 September, Hong Kong's High Court sentenced three organizers of the city's annual Tiananmen vigil — Chow Hang-tung, Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho — to five to seven years in prison for inciting subversion under the National Security Law, and fined their organization, the Hong Kong Alliance, HK$1.5 million. The judges themselves said the case did not involve violence or the threat of violence. The United Nations Human Rights Office called the outcome "another regrettable outcome of the deeply flawed National Security Law," and its head, Volker Türk, called for the sentences to be quashed. The next day, Hong Kong's government rejected the criticism, saying the court reached its verdicts "fairly and impartially...free from any interference or political consideration," and defended the law itself as protecting "leadership by the Communist Party of China" as "the core of the fundamental system." This is the third escalation the benchmark has tracked in the same pattern since a 21 August watch flag: after earlier bookstore raids and the prosecution of a vigil organizer with an intellectual disability, this sentencing lands within the four-month escalation window that flag anticipated. Hong Kong's score falls 5.9 points, from 32.8 to 26.9 of 100, remaining in the Developing band.

evidence.quote: In the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, today's imposition of lengthy jail terms on three activists and a heavy fine on the affiliated civil society organisation is another regrettable outcome of the deeply flawed National Security Law.
evidence.claim: The UN Human Rights Office characterized the sentences as a regrettable outcome of a deeply flawed law.

evidence.quote: The court reached its verdicts and sentences fairly and impartially on the basis of law and evidence, free from any interference or political consideration.
evidence.claim: Hong Kong's government denied any political influence over the sentencing and dismissed the international criticism.

evidence.quote: did not involve violence or the threat of violence
evidence.claim: The court itself acknowledged the offense involved no violence, even as it imposed multi-year prison terms.

evidence.quote: The conviction of these Tiananmen vigil organizers shows that public displays of mourning have become a crime in Hong Kong.
evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch had already characterized the underlying conviction as criminalizing public mourning, the pattern this sentencing escalates.

topSignals.title: France and Slovenia Would Both Cross Into a Lower Band — Neither Finding Cleared the Bar to Confirm It
topSignals.whyItMatters: Both countries show real conduct that would cross a scoring boundary. Neither crossing was confirmed, because the sourcing behind each fell short of the strength the benchmark requires.
topSignals.description:
France's published score, 62.5 of 100, had never been individually reviewed before. The most prominent evidence this cycle — a protest movement reported at nearly 200,000 people and hundreds of arrests — turned out to date from September 2025, a full year before this review window, and was excluded once the dates were checked directly. What survived is smaller but real: on 13 September, France's UN mission in Geneva said it "regretted" a July social-media post that had criticized the United States over human rights, a dispute that had delayed France's new ambassador to Washington taking up the post. The US State Department responded that it "noted and appreciated" the statement. That finding moves France's score by about one point on its own. Measured against all located evidence, most of it predating this review window, France's score comes out at 52.5, crossing from the Established band into Functional — but the finding rests on a single tier-2 news source, well short of the court, UN, or international-organization-level source the benchmark requires to confirm a boundary crossing, so the finding was not filed.

Slovenia's published score, also 62.5, faced a similar test on different evidence. Slovenia's new government scrapped its predecessor's arms embargo and settlement-goods import ban on Israel and welcomed the opening of Israel's first embassy in Slovenia, reversing course entirely on the prior government's position. Al Jazeera reported that "all prior measures on Israel were scrapped wholesale on the change of government," and that the Palestinian flag was removed from government buildings. Measured against that reversal, Slovenia's score would fall to 58.7, also crossing into Functional — 1.3 points below the boundary. But the source base is a tier-2 news report and a tier-1 digital-rights organization's update describing amendments that have not been confirmed as enacted, not a court or international body's finding, so this crossing was withheld as well.

evidence.claim: France's UN mission in Geneva characterized its retracted human-rights criticism of the United States as concerning a single vote.

evidence.quote: We note and appreciate France's statement, and look forward to working together to further shared values and interests
evidence.claim: The United States accepted France's retraction of its human-rights criticism.

evidence.quote: all prior measures on Israel were scrapped wholesale on the change of government
evidence.claim: Slovenia's new government reversed its predecessor's Israel policy in full, including an arms embargo and a settlement-goods import ban.

evidence.quote: expand surveillance, legalise the use of spyware, and open the door to serious intrusions into privacy
evidence.claim: A European digital-rights organization flagged surveillance-expanding amendments in Slovenia that have not been confirmed as enacted.

topSignals.title: Nepal's Flood Death Toll Reaches 1,386 — the Score Has Now Measured Below Its Published Level Twice Running
topSignals.whyItMatters: Nepal's flood death toll keeps rising, and the government's own emergency-alert system still failed to warn people in time. This is the second cycle in a row the measured score has come in below what's published.
topSignals.description: Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority now counts 1,386 people dead and about 5,130 still missing from the flash floods, as of 12-13 September — the toll has been revised upward three times since 1 September. The government mobilized 21,465 security personnel and 1,348 rescue flights within the first ten days, a large-scale response, but the emergency SMS alert system arrived with the flood itself rather than ahead of it, and only in Nepali, leaving non-Nepali speakers without warning. A binding rule connecting weather forecasts to mandatory evacuation action, recommended after a 2021 disaster, still has not been implemented. Nepal's measured score is 43.8 of 100, 4.6 points below its published 48.4 — the second consecutive cycle the measured figure has landed below the published one, though not enough on its own to trigger a finding. The country remains in the Functional band.

evidence.claim: Nepal's disaster-management authority's rolling death toll from the flash floods, as of 12-13 September.
evidence.source: Akashvani / All India Radio News, citing Nepal's NDRRMA

evidence.quote: The SMS and the flood came together
evidence.claim: Nepal's official emergency alert reached residents at the same time as the flood itself, not ahead of it.

topSignals.title: Jamaica's Hurricane Housing Program Is Confirmed: 268 Homes, About US$6.6 Million
topSignals.whyItMatters: A hurricane-relief program is real but small: 268 new homes against roughly 24,000 destroyed. The earlier reported figure was in the wrong currency, overstating the scale by a factor of about 150.
topSignals.description: Jamaica signed contracts worth 1.05 billion Jamaican dollars, about US$6.6 million, to deliver 268 semi-permanent homes to families displaced by Hurricane Melissa, with beneficiaries verified by the Ministry of Labour and Social Security. Completion is scheduled within twelve months, though no occupancy-tracking plan has been documented yet. The figure is real progress, but small measured against the storm's scale: roughly 24,000 homes were destroyed. Jamaica's score is confirmed at 37.5 of 100, remaining in the Developing band.

evidence.quote: beneficiaries were verified by the Ministry of Labour and Social Security
evidence.claim: Jamaica's housing-relief beneficiaries for the 268-home program underwent a documented verification process this year.

topSignals.title: Syria Holds at Zero as Fuel Prices Jump Up to 40 Percent Overnight and Protests Spread
topSignals.whyItMatters: Syria's score is already the lowest possible score, zero of 100. A new fuel-price shock hitting a population where nine in ten people live below the poverty line has no further room to register as a decline.
topSignals.description: Diesel prices rose as much as 40 percent and petrol 28 percent overnight on 12-13 September, in a country where about 90 percent of people live below the poverty line. Protests broke out across multiple cities. Syria's Ministry of Energy said only that it would continue to review prices; no relief measure for the poorest households was announced. Some legislative scrutiny did occur — the People's Assembly summoned the Energy Minister to a hearing to explain the increases. Syria's score measures at 0.6 of 100, effectively unchanged from its published 0.0, which is already the floor of the benchmark's scale. A real, evidenced decline in a population's welfare has no further room to move a score that is already at zero.

evidence.quote: diesel rose up to 40% and petrol 28% overnight on 12-13 September
evidence.claim: Syria's fuel prices jumped sharply overnight in a country where about 90 percent of the population lives below the poverty line.

evidence.quote: protests break out across Syria over fuel price increases
evidence.claim: Fuel-price protests spread across multiple Syrian cities in response to the overnight price increases.

topSignals.title: Spain's Score, Measured Independently Tonight, Lines Up With a Downgrade Still Awaiting a Decision
topSignals.whyItMatters: A finding filed three weeks ago about Spain's response to a migration crisis in Ceuta gets independent support tonight, without a second finding being filed on top of it.
topSignals.description: Spain's score measures at 51.2 of 100 tonight, within six tenths of a point of a downgrade already filed on 26 August that proposed 50.6 — both measurements point to the same conclusion from Spain's response to the Ceuta migrant crisis, so no second, duplicate finding was filed. New in-window information adds a small positive detail: Spain did not summarily deport unaccompanied migrant children this cycle, and transferred about 500 children to the mainland instead. Spain's published score, 60.0 of 100, sits exactly on the line between the benchmark's Functional and Established bands. The pending finding, if resolved, would move the score further into the Functional band rather than change which side of that line Spain sits on.

evidence.quote: Thousands of people have been in the streets in a legal vacuum, exposed to sexual violence and without adequate shelter, food, or sanitation for almost three weeks.
evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch documented conditions for migrants left unsheltered in Ceuta, the basis for the pending 26 August finding this cycle corroborates.

evidence.quote: Spain says more than 5,300 migrants have left Ceuta for Morocco
evidence.claim: Independent, more recent reporting on the state of the Ceuta migrant population, cited for context on the pace of returns.

topSignals.title: Boeing's Score Holds at 14.1 — the New Fact Is a Fine's Disclosure Timing, Not New Misconduct
topSignals.whyItMatters: A $3.1 million FAA fine for a safety-compliance violation was paid quietly in January and only became public in September, when a reporter asked. The delay itself, not a new violation, is what moved the score slightly.
topSignals.description: The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed to Reuters on 2 September that Boeing paid a $3.1 million fine in January 2026, after a Boeing employee pressured a colleague performing FAA-delegated inspection work to sign off a non-compliant 737 MAX in order to meet a delivery schedule. Boeing confirmed paying the fine but gave no further comment. Counted in Boeing's favor: the FAA lifted its 38-per-month production cap in October 2025 and, in July 2026, restored Boeing's authority to issue its own airworthiness certificates after sustained proof of consistent production quality — though that improvement happened before this review window and is not itself the basis for any upward move. Boeing's score is confirmed at 14.1 of 100, remaining in the Critical band.

evidence.claim: The FAA finding, confirmed in-window, describes a delivery schedule prioritized over a compliance determination.

boundaryWatch.trigger: A court, UN body, or international-organization finding on 2026 conduct would be needed before this crossing could move from a documented finding to a filed proposal.
boundaryWatch.note: France sits at its published score of 62.5 of 100, 2.5 points above the Functional boundary, in its first individual review. A measured reading of 52.5 would cross into Functional, but most of that movement reflects evidence from before this review window, and the widely reported protest evidence turned out to date from September 2025 and was excluded. The one surviving in-window finding, a diplomatic retraction, rests on a single tier-2 source. Published score unchanged.

boundaryWatch.trigger: Confirmation from a court or international body that Slovenia's surveillance-related legislative amendments have been enacted, rather than merely proposed, would meet the evidence bar this finding currently fails.
boundaryWatch.note: Slovenia sits at its published score of 62.5 of 100, 2.5 points above the Functional boundary, in its first individual review. A measured reading of 58.7 — just 1.3 points below the boundary — reflects a reversal of the prior government's Israel policy, but rests on tier-1 and tier-2 sourcing rather than a court or international-organization finding. Published score unchanged.

boundaryWatch.trigger: Publication of the results of the police-commander hearing Human Rights Watch referenced would be the next accountability test for Mozambique's record.
boundaryWatch.note: Mozambique sits at its published score of 23.4 of 100 in its first individual review. A measured reading of 21.3 — 1.3 points above the Critical floor — reflects documented impunity for roughly 400 killings during last year's post-election unrest. Published score unchanged.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries — Two Withheld Boundary Crossings and a Flood Toll Still Rising
sectorAlerts.headline: France and Slovenia both show conduct that would cross into a lower band, but neither crossing cleared the benchmark's sourcing bar; Nepal's toll and Syria's floor both moved without changing a published score.
observations: France (62.5 published, 52.5 measured): the year's most-reported protest evidence dated to 2025, not 2026, and was excluded; the surviving finding is a single diplomatic retraction.
Slovenia (62.5 published, 58.7 measured): a full reversal of the prior government's Israel policy is real, but rests on tier-1 and tier-2 sourcing, short of the bar for a confirmed crossing.
Spain (60.0 published, 51.2 measured): corroborates a pending 26 August finding within six tenths of a point; no second finding was filed.
Nepal (48.4 published, 43.8 measured): the flood death toll reached 1,386 and has been revised upward three times in under two weeks.
Jamaica (37.5 published, 36.9 measured): a housing-relief figure that could be misread as US dollars was verified as 1.05 billion Jamaican dollars (about US$6.6 million) before use.
Syria (0.0 published, 0.6 measured): fuel prices jumped sharply and protests spread; the floor score has no room left to register the decline.
Mozambique (23.4 published, 21.3 measured, first individual review): documented impunity for about 400 killings sits the country 1.3 points above the Critical floor.
Bolivia, Brazil, Cabo Verde, Liechtenstein, Uruguay, Portugal, Poland, South Korea and Indonesia all confirmed within a small margin of their published scores.

Boeing (14.1 published, 12.5 confirmed): a $3.1 million FAA fine paid in January became public only in September; the disclosure timing, not new conduct, moved the score slightly.

methodologyNotes.name: A Band Crossing Needs a Strong Source, Not Just a Large Number
methodologyNotes.description: France and Slovenia both measured a fall large enough to cross from the Established band into Functional this cycle. Neither crossing was confirmed. The benchmark requires at least one source at the strength of a court, a UN body, or an international organization before a crossing between bands is filed — and in both cases, the sourcing available fell short of that bar, even though the underlying conduct is real and documented at a lower source tier.

methodologyNotes.name: A Disclosure Date Is Not a Conduct Date
methodologyNotes.description: Boeing's federal fine was paid in January 2026 but only became public in September, when a regulator confirmed it to a reporter. The benchmark scores the disclosure timing as its own fact, separate from the underlying conduct the fine addressed. A company that discloses slowly is scored differently from one that discloses promptly, even when the underlying violation is identical.

methodologyNotes.name: Currency Units Are Verified, Not Assumed
methodologyNotes.description: A housing-relief figure for Jamaica was reported in a way that could be read as US dollars. Verified against primary reporting, the figure is 1.05 billion Jamaican dollars, about US$6.6 million — roughly 150 times smaller than a misreading would suggest. The figure was checked in its original currency before it was used.
